findings.title: SSE hub broadcasts auth:revoked with another user's Discord ID to every connected dashboard session
findings.root_cause: auth:revoked events carry { userId } but no ownerId, and the only userId comparison is the early-return that terminates the *matching* user's stream. A non-matching auth:revoked falls through every remaining filter (no ownerId, no botId) and is written verbatim to the subscriber.
findings.violated_invariant: A dashboard principal must only receive events concerning resources or identities they are authorized to see.
findings.data_flow: Admin calls POST /api/admin/tokens or DELETE /api/admin/tokens/:userId (or a Discord admin runs /new-token, /renew-token, /del-token) -> tokenService.issueToken/renewToken/revokeToken -> publish('auth:revoked', { userId }) -> eventHub emit -> every subscribed SSE response in events.js -> writeEvent to all authenticated browsers.
attack_scenario: Attacker holds any valid, non-admin dashboard token and opens the dashboard, establishing GET /api/events.
An administrator issues, renews, or revokes a token for any other Discord user.
The attacker's EventSource receives event: auth:revoked with data {"userId":"<victim Discord snowflake>"}.
Repeating passively over time, the attacker enumerates the Discord user IDs of every dashboard account and observes administrative token activity timing.
findings.preconditions: One valid session cookie; an admin performing any token operation while the attacker is connected.
findings.affected_deployment: Any deployment with more than one dashboard user.

impact.confidentiality: Discloses other users' Discord user IDs (PII/identifier) and administrative token-lifecycle activity.
impact.business_impact: Leaks the operator's user roster and admin activity pattern; useful for targeted social engineering against Discord accounts that control the bot fleet.

reproduction.type: local deterministic PoC (no network, mocked req/res)
steps: Set dummy env: ENCRYPTION_KEY=<64 hex>, ADMIN_USER_IDS=<snowflake>, DISCORD_TOKEN=<dummy>, DISCORD_CLIENT_ID=<dummy>.
require src/web/routes/events.js, build the router with a stub botManager whose listAuthorizedBots() returns [].
Invoke the route handler with a fake req { principal: { userId: 'victim-1' }, session: { expiresAt: +60s } } and a fake res capturing write().
Call publish('auth:revoked', { userId: 'someone-else-2' }) from src/web/sse/eventHub.js.
reproduction.expected_result: No frame is written to victim-1's stream, or the frame is scrubbed of the foreign userId.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Executed entirely in-process against stub objects; no HTTP listener, no database, no Discord.

findings.existing_controls: sanitizeEventData() strips only ownerId, not userId. tests/ contains no assertion that auth:revoked is scoped, so the regression suite does not catch this.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: In onEvent, treat auth:* events as strictly user-scoped: if event.event startsWith 'auth:' and event.data?.userId !== req.principal.userId, return without writing. Additionally have sanitizeEventData drop userId from any outbound payload.
alternatives: Change publish() to route auth events on a per-user channel keyed by userId instead of the global 'event' channel.
Deliver revocation out-of-band by closing the affected user's activeStreams entry directly instead of broadcasting.
regression_tests: Assert that a subscriber for user A receives nothing when auth:revoked is published for user B.
Assert that user A's stream still terminates on its own auth:revoked.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No SSE frame containing a foreign userId is ever written; the self-revocation termination path is unchanged.

findings.auto_fix_reason: The change is a narrow filter addition in one function with clear, testable semantics and no cross-module contract change.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Disproof attempted by checking whether sanitizeEventData or the ownerId filter removes userId — it does not (it deletes only ownerId), and auth:revoked payloads contain no ownerId or botId, so both remaining guards are no-ops. The PoC output confirms delivery.
findings.limitations: The PoC bypasses the authenticate middleware by invoking the final handler directly; in production the attacker simply needs a valid cookie, which is the stated precondition.

findings.title: bot:created SSE events are exempted from the visibility filter, leaking other users' bot snapshots
findings.category: Broken access control / IDOR on an event stream
findings.root_cause: The visibility check explicitly excludes bot:created so that a user's own new bot can be added to visibleBotIds. Correctness therefore depends entirely on the preceding ownerId guard, which is conditional on ownerId being present (`event.data?.ownerId &&`). Any bot:created publication that omits ownerId is delivered to every subscriber together with the full snapshot.
findings.violated_invariant: Bot snapshots must only reach the principal whose userId equals record.createdBy.
findings.data_flow: BotManager.createBot -> publish('bot:created', { botId, ownerId, snapshot }) (ownerId present, safe today) ; but src/web/sse/WebNotifier.js publishCreated() publishes { snapshot } with NO ownerId, and eventHub is a process-global emitter, so any future or partial wiring of WebNotifier fans a foreign snapshot to all subscribers.
attack_scenario: A subscriber with any valid session keeps GET /api/events open.
A bot:created (or any event) is published without an ownerId field — currently possible via createWebNotifier().publishCreated/publishUpdated.
The subscriber receives the full snapshot (id, host, port, username, label, version, state, position) of a bot owned by a different user.
findings.preconditions: A publisher path that omits ownerId. WebNotifier is currently not wired into the running app (no importers found), which is why this is 'likely' rather than 'confirmed'.
findings.affected_deployment: Multi-user dashboards; becomes immediately exploitable the moment WebNotifier is connected or another publisher forgets ownerId.

impact.confidentiality: Full bot inventory disclosure across tenants (target Minecraft server host/port, in-game username, live position).
impact.business_impact: Reveals which Minecraft servers and accounts the operator runs, enabling targeted in-game griefing or account attacks.

steps: Inspect src/web/sse/WebNotifier.js:46-54 — publishCreated/publishUpdated/publishDeleted emit payloads with no ownerId.
Inspect src/web/routes/events.js:69 — the ownerId guard is skipped entirely when ownerId is undefined.
Inspect src/web/routes/events.js:71 — bot:created is explicitly excluded from the visibleBotIds check.
reproduction.expected_result: Events lacking ownerId are denied by default.
reproduction.observed_result: Events lacking ownerId are allowed by default (fail-open filter).
reproduction.poc_constraints: A runtime PoC would require wiring WebNotifier, which would mean modifying source — prohibited during the audit pass. Static proof only.

findings.existing_controls: instanceEvents.js and BotManager consistently include ownerId today, which is the only reason this is not currently exploitable.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Make the filter fail-closed: require an ownerId on every bot:* event and drop the event when it is absent or does not match; keep the bot:created exemption only for events whose ownerId equals the principal.
alternatives: Publish to per-user topics rather than a global emitter.
Delete the unused WebNotifier module so only the ownerId-carrying publishers exist (see EG-016).
regression_tests: Publish bot:created without ownerId and assert nothing is written to any subscriber.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No bot snapshot is delivered to a principal that does not own it, regardless of publisher.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Making the filter fail-closed could suppress legitimate events if some publisher is later found to intentionally omit ownerId; a maintainer should confirm the publisher contract.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Attempted disproof by enumerating all publish('bot:created'...) call sites: BotManager.js:180 includes ownerId, WebNotifier.js:47 does not. Because WebNotifier has no importers, no live exploit exists at this commit — hence status 'likely' and reachable=false, not 'confirmed'.
findings.limitations: Reachability depends on wiring that does not exist at this commit.

findings.title: Dashboard bearer JWTs are transmitted through Discord messages and rendered in the browser
findings.root_cause: The long-lived (up to 365-day) session credential is delivered as plaintext chat content to a third-party platform, and is also returned in the JSON body of POST /api/admin/tokens for in-page display.
findings.violated_invariant: Long-lived authentication credentials should not be persisted in third-party message stores or rendered where they can be shoulder-surfed, screenshotted, or cached.
findings.data_flow: issueTokenDays() -> jwt.sign -> interaction.editReply (Discord ephemeral message, stored by Discord) ; and adminTokens POST -> res.json({ token }) -> TokenManagementPage renders {newToken}.
attack_scenario: An operator with access to the admin's Discord client, a synced session, or Discord message history recovers the ephemeral reply content.
Alternatively a screenshot, clipboard manager, or browser memory dump captures the rendered token.
The token authenticates directly at POST /api/auth/login for its full remaining TTL unless explicitly revoked.
findings.attacker_role: Anyone with incidental access to the admin's Discord client or screen
findings.preconditions: Admin performs /new-token or /renew-token, or uses the token management page.

impact.confidentiality: Full dashboard account takeover for the affected user.
impact.integrity: Attacker can create/edit/delete that user's bots.
impact.availability: Attacker can stop the user's bots.
impact.blast_radius: One user account per leaked token; an admin's token yields token-management privileges.
impact.business_impact: Account takeover of the control plane.

steps: Read src/discord/commands/new-token.js:26-40 and src/web/routes/adminTokens.js:24-38.
reproduction.expected_result: Credential delivered over a channel designed for secrets, or one-time-view with short TTL.
reproduction.observed_result: Raw JWT embedded in a Discord message body and in an API JSON response.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No live Discord interaction was performed, per the safety rules.

findings.existing_controls: Replies use MessageFlags.Ephemeral, and the token hash (not the token) is stored server-side; revocation is supported. Maximum TTL is 365 days, which lengthens exposure.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Lower the default and maximum TTL substantially (e.g. 7-30 days), and document that /new-token output must be treated as a password. Consider requiring the recipient to redeem a short-lived one-time claim code instead of the JWT itself.
alternatives: DM-only delivery with a short redemption window
Discord OAuth2 login replacing manual tokens entirely
regression_tests: Assert MAX_TOKEN_TTL_DAYS enforcement at the new, lower bound.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No credential with a multi-month lifetime is delivered through chat.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Changing the credential distribution model is a product decision that affects operator workflow.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Not a false positive: the token is a bearer credential accepted at /api/auth/login with no second factor. Ephemeral flags reduce but do not eliminate exposure.
findings.limitations: Exposure depends on the operator's Discord hygiene.

findings.title: No CSRF defence on cookie-authenticated state-changing endpoints beyond SameSite=Lax
findings.excerpt: return { httpOnly: true, secure: config.web.https, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge };
findings.root_cause: Authentication is ambient (cookie) and there is no CSRF token, no Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch-Site validation, and no custom-header requirement. SameSite=Lax is the sole mitigation.
findings.violated_invariant: State-changing requests must be provably initiated by the application's own origin.
findings.data_flow: Attacker page -> cross-site request carrying eg_session -> express -> authenticate() -> BotManager mutation.
attack_scenario: A logged-in dashboard user visits an attacker page.
Lax blocks cross-site POST with cookies in current mainstream browsers, so a plain form POST fails.

Residual risk: browsers or embedded webviews that do not enforce Lax-by-default, a same-site-but-different-subdomain attacker (Lax is site-scoped, not origin-scoped), or any future GET-based mutation. In those cases /api/bots (create), PATCH/DELETE /api/bots/:id, and /api/bots/:id/{start,stop,restart,chat} execute with the victim's identity.
findings.attacker_role: Web attacker controlling any page the victim visits, or any subdomain of the dashboard's registrable domain
findings.preconditions: Victim has an active eg_session cookie.
findings.affected_deployment: Deployments where the dashboard shares a registrable domain with less-trusted content, or where clients are legacy/webview.

impact.confidentiality: Limited — responses are not readable cross-origin without CORS (none is configured, which is correct).
impact.integrity: Bot creation, edit, deletion, and in-game chat sent as the victim.
impact.business_impact: Unauthorized in-game actions and loss of bot configuration.

steps: grep the codebase for csrf/xsrf/Origin checks — none exist; confirm cookieOptions sameSite value.
reproduction.expected_result: A synchronizer token or origin check on unsafe methods.
reproduction.poc_constraints: A browser-based PoC would require a live deployment and a second origin; not performed.

findings.existing_controls: SameSite=Lax; JSON-only body parsing (a simple HTML form cannot set Content-Type: application/json, and express.json ignores other types — this is a meaningful additional barrier for POST/PATCH).

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Reject unsafe-method requests whose Origin (or Sec-Fetch-Site) header is not same-origin; this is a few lines of middleware and requires no frontend change.
alternatives: Double-submit CSRF cookie plus X-CSRF-Token header
Switch cookie to SameSite=Strict where the UX permits
regression_tests: Assert 403 for a POST /api/bots carrying a foreign Origin header and a valid cookie.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Unsafe methods succeed only with a same-origin Origin header.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Origin enforcement can break non-browser API clients or proxy setups that strip Origin; the deployment's client mix must be confirmed.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Partially mitigated rather than absent: Lax plus JSON-only parsing makes classic form CSRF impractical on modern browsers. Severity is therefore Medium, not High.
findings.limitations: Real-world exploitability depends heavily on browser and domain topology.

findings.title: Express trust proxy is never configured, so the login rate limiter keys on the proxy IP
findings.root_cause: The documented deployment terminates TLS at Cloudflare and proxies to the Node origin, but Express is left with trust proxy disabled. express-rate-limit therefore derives its key from req.ip, which is the proxy's socket address for every request.
findings.violated_invariant: Per-client throttling must key on the actual client identity.
findings.data_flow: Client -> Cloudflare -> Node socket (proxy IP) -> req.ip -> loginLimiter key.
attack_scenario: All traffic arrives from a small set of Cloudflare egress IPs.

The 10-per-15-minute login limit becomes a single global bucket: one attacker exhausts it and denies login to every legitimate user (DoS), while distributed attackers each still get throttled collectively rather than individually.
Conversely, if a future change enables trust proxy without restricting it to the known proxy, X-Forwarded-For becomes attacker-controlled and the limiter is trivially bypassed per-request.
findings.preconditions: Deployment behind a reverse proxy, which docs/cloudflare-reverse-proxy.md describes as the intended topology.

impact.availability: Login can be denied to all users by exhausting the shared bucket.
impact.business_impact: Lockout of legitimate operators; degraded brute-force protection granularity.

steps: grep -rn "trust proxy" src -> no results.
Read src/web/routes/auth.js:11-17 (limiter with default keyGenerator).
reproduction.expected_result: app.set('trust proxy', <specific hop count or proxy list>) when deployed behind a proxy.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Behaviour is topology-dependent; not reproduced against a live proxy.

findings.existing_controls: The limiter itself exists and is correctly scoped to the login route.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Add a WEB_TRUST_PROXY env setting and call app.set('trust proxy', value) with a specific hop count or CIDR list — never the boolean true.
alternatives: Key the login limiter on the submitted token prefix/user rather than IP
Enforce rate limiting at the edge (Cloudflare)
regression_tests: Assert req.ip resolves to the forwarded client when the trust setting is configured and to the socket address when it is not.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: The limiter keys on the real client IP in the documented topology, and X-Forwarded-For from untrusted hops is ignored.

findings.auto_fix_reason: The correct trust-proxy value depends on the operator's actual hop count; a wrong value converts a DoS issue into a bypass.
findings.false_positive_analysis: For a direct-to-Internet HTTP deployment (also supported), the current setting is correct — hence Medium and not High.
findings.limitations: Depends on deployment topology not visible in the repository.

findings.title: ENCRYPTION_KEY is reused as the JWT signing secret, coupling credential encryption to session signing
findings.root_cause: One secret serves two cryptographic purposes with different lifecycles: AES-256-GCM data-at-rest encryption (which supports rotation via OLD_ENCRYPTION_KEY) and HMAC-SHA256 JWT signing (which has no rotation path here).
findings.violated_invariant: Distinct cryptographic purposes require distinct keys; key rotation for one purpose must not silently invalidate or weaken the other.
findings.data_flow: process.env.ENCRYPTION_KEY -> config.encryption.key (AES-GCM for Minecraft passwords) and -> tokenService.secret() (HMAC for all dashboard JWTs).
attack_scenario: Operator follows the documented rotation procedure: set OLD_ENCRYPTION_KEY, set a new ENCRYPTION_KEY, restart. Stored passwords are re-encrypted correctly.
Every outstanding dashboard JWT silently fails verification, logging out all users — an availability surprise not documented anywhere.
Conversely, any disclosure of the JWT signing secret (e.g. through a future logging or error-path regression) also grants the ability to decrypt every stored Minecraft credential, and vice versa.
findings.attacker_role: Any attacker who obtains one secret through any path
findings.preconditions: Disclosure of ENCRYPTION_KEY through any channel.

impact.confidentiality: A single key compromise yields both forged sessions (full dashboard impersonation of any userId, since normalizeUserId only checks the digit shape) and decryption of all stored Minecraft passwords.
impact.integrity: Forged JWTs allow arbitrary bot mutation.
impact.availability: Key rotation logs out every user without warning.
impact.business_impact: Maximally amplified impact of any single secret leak.

steps: Compare src/config/index.js:54-85 with src/web/auth/tokenService.js:12-18.
reproduction.expected_result: A dedicated JWT_SECRET / SESSION_SECRET env var.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No forged token was produced; doing so with a real key is out of scope and unnecessary — the coupling is evident from the code.

findings.existing_controls: The key is validated as 32 bytes of hex, which is adequate entropy for HS256. Tokens are additionally bound to a DB row hash, so a forged JWT alone does not authenticate — verifyActiveToken also requires a matching token_hash row. This materially reduces the forgery impact and is why the severity is Medium rather than High.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Introduce a separate required env var (e.g. WEB_JWT_SECRET), fall back to ENCRYPTION_KEY only with a startup warning for backward compatibility, and document the rotation consequence.
alternatives: Derive a purpose-separated subkey with HKDF from a single master secret, using distinct info labels.
regression_tests: Assert that changing ENCRYPTION_KEY alone does not invalidate sessions once the dedicated secret exists.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Encryption and signing use independently rotatable key material.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Adding a required env var is a breaking deployment change; the fallback strategy needs an operator decision.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Not a false positive, but impact is bounded by the DB-side token_hash check, which means a forged JWT is rejected unless the attacker can also insert the matching hash row.
findings.limitations: Impact assessment assumes the DB is not simultaneously compromised.

findings.title: jwt.verify is called without an algorithms allowlist
findings.root_cause: No { algorithms: ['HS256'] } option is supplied, so the accepted algorithm set is whatever the library defaults to for a string secret.
findings.violated_invariant: Token verification must pin the expected signature algorithm.
attack_scenario: With jsonwebtoken 9.x a string secret already restricts verification to HMAC families and 'none' is rejected, so no practical confusion exists today.

The residual risk is regression: a future refactor that passes a key object or a downgrade to a permissive version reintroduces algorithm confusion, where an attacker signs a token with a different algorithm accepted by the same key material.
findings.attacker_role: Unauthenticated attacker holding a crafted token
findings.preconditions: A change in library version or key type.

impact.confidentiality: Would be full authentication bypass if the latent condition were met.

steps: Read src/web/auth/tokenService.js:124-132; confirm no options object.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No exploit exists against jsonwebtoken 9.0.3 with a string secret; asserting otherwise would be inaccurate.

findings.existing_controls: jsonwebtoken 9.0.3 (per lockfile) rejects 'none' and restricts HMAC verification for string secrets; the DB token_hash check is a second gate.

alternatives: Also pin issuer/audience claims.
regression_tests: Assert a token signed with a non-HS256 algorithm is rejected.

findings.auto_fix_reason: One-line, behaviour-preserving hardening with an obvious test.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Deliberately rated Low and 'likely' (not confirmed) because the installed library version already prevents the classic attack; claiming an exploitable bypass would be inflation.

findings.title: Only the login route is rate limited; authenticated API and SSE endpoints have no request throttling
findings.root_cause: express-rate-limit is applied only inside createAuthRouter for POST /login. No global limiter, no per-route limiter, and no cap on concurrent SSE streams across users.
findings.violated_invariant: Every externally reachable endpoint must have a bounded request cost.
attack_scenario: Unauthenticated flood of /healthz or the SPA fallback route saturates the event loop and the log streams.
An authenticated user opens GET /api/bots/:id repeatedly; each call serialises up to 200 buffered log lines.

Each SSE connection registers a listener on a process-global EventEmitter with setMaxListeners(0) and a 20s keepalive interval. activeStreams caps one stream per user, but the number of distinct token-holding users is unbounded from the server's perspective, and a user can churn connections to force repeated initial-snapshot replays.
findings.attacker_role: Unauthenticated attacker (public routes) or any authenticated token holder (API/SSE)
findings.affected_deployment: All, especially the compose default that publishes the port on 0.0.0.0.

impact.availability: CPU/memory/socket exhaustion; degraded or unavailable dashboard and, through event-loop starvation, degraded bot supervision.
impact.blast_radius: Whole process (bots and dashboard share one Node process).

reproduction.type: static analysis (no load generated, per safety rules)
steps: grep -rn rateLimit src/web -> only src/web/routes/auth.js.
Read src/web/server.js:52-64.
reproduction.expected_result: A baseline global limiter plus a stricter one on expensive endpoints.

findings.existing_controls: express.json 32kb body cap; per-user chat cooldown and bot-creation sliding window in BotManager; one SSE stream per user; per-bot queue bounds.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Mount a conservative global express-rate-limit before the routers (after fixing trust proxy per EG-005), and a tighter limiter on /api/events and /api/bots.
alternatives: Edge rate limiting at Cloudflare
Per-principal concurrency accounting
regression_tests: Assert 429 after N requests within the window on a protected route.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Every route has an enforced request budget.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Limits interact with SSE long-polling semantics and with the trust-proxy fix; thresholds need operator input.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Partially mitigated by application-level per-user limits on the expensive bot operations, which is why this is Medium rather than High.

findings.title: Chat rate limit is consumed before authorization, letting an unauthorized caller burn another action's budget and probe timing
findings.root_cause: consumeChat() mutates limiter state before resolveAuthorizedBot() verifies the caller may address the bot at all, so failed authorization still consumes the caller's own quota.
findings.violated_invariant: Authorization should precede resource accounting, and a denied request should not alter shared state.
findings.data_flow: POST /api/bots/:botId/chat or /chat slash command -> chatBot -> consumeChat (state mutation) -> resolveAuthorizedBot (may throw).
attack_scenario: A user repeatedly issues chat requests against bot IDs they do not own.
Each request consumes their own cooldown slot even though the operation fails, and the differing latency/error between RATE_LIMITED and RESOURCE_ACCESS_DENIED gives a weak signal about ordering.
Self-inflicted denial only — the limiter is keyed on the caller's own userId, so no cross-user impact exists.

impact.confidentiality: Negligible; error codes already avoid confirming resource existence (RESOURCE_ACCESS_DENIED maps to a generic 404 'Bot not found.').
impact.availability: Self-denial of the caller's own chat quota.

steps: Read src/manager/BotManager.js:300-309 and compare with createBot, which also consumes before validating.
reproduction.poc_constraints: None needed; the ordering is unambiguous.

findings.existing_controls: mapError normalises RESOURCE_ACCESS_DENIED to a generic 404, preventing existence oracles.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Resolve and authorize the bot first, then consume the limiter.
alternatives: Refund the limiter slot when authorization fails.
regression_tests: Assert that a chat attempt against a foreign bot leaves the caller's cooldown untouched.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Denied requests do not consume quota.

findings.auto_fix_reason: A two-statement reordering within one function with no external contract change.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Impact is genuinely low because the limiter is per-caller; this is recorded as correctness/defence-in-depth rather than an access-control break.

findings.title: Rate-limiter maps grow without bound, retaining an entry per user id forever
findings.root_cause: Entries are only removed by an explicit clear(key), and grep shows clear() is never called anywhere in the codebase. Unlike LogBuffers, there is no periodic prune or size cap.
findings.violated_invariant: Unbounded per-identity state must have an eviction policy.
findings.data_flow: Every chat and every bot-creation attempt inserts/updates a Map entry keyed by the caller's Discord snowflake; the process is long-lived (restart: unless-stopped).
attack_scenario: Any authenticated user issues chat or create-bot attempts; each distinct userId permanently occupies a Map slot.
The SlidingWindowRateLimiter additionally retains a timestamp array per key, filtered on read but never deleted, so the key set only grows.
Growth is bounded in practice by the number of distinct token holders, so this is slow-burn rather than a direct DoS.
findings.attacker_role: Authenticated user (or an operator with many issued tokens)
findings.preconditions: Long process uptime and many distinct users.

steps: grep -rn "\.clear(" src | verify no caller for the limiter clear methods.
Compare with src/services/logBuffer.js which does implement pruning.
reproduction.expected_result: TTL-based eviction or a size cap.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Demonstrating growth would require a long-running load test; not performed.

findings.existing_controls: None for these maps. LogBuffers demonstrates the pattern the project already uses elsewhere.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Add an unref'd periodic prune that deletes entries older than the window (mirroring LogBuffers.pruneCooldowns), plus a hard entry cap.
alternatives: Use an LRU with a fixed capacity.
regression_tests: Assert map size shrinks after advancing a fake clock past the window.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Limiter memory is bounded by active users, not lifetime users.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Self-contained additive change to one small module with an established in-repo precedent.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Real but slow; correctly rated Low. Not a remote DoS because key creation requires a valid session.

findings.title: Container image copies the full build context as root-owned application code and lacks runtime hardening
findings.excerpt:
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=web-build /app/web/dist ./web/dist
COPY . .
RUN mkdir -p /app/logs && chown -R node:node /app
USER node
VOLUME ["/app/logs"]
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["npm", "run", "start"]
findings.root_cause: chown -R node:node /app makes the entire application tree, including source and node_modules, writable by the runtime user. There is no read-only root filesystem, no cap_drop, no no-new-privileges, and no HEALTHCHECK.
findings.violated_invariant: A compromised runtime process should not be able to modify the code it executes.
findings.data_flow: Any code-execution foothold in the Node process -> write to /app/*.js -> persistence across container restarts is limited (image layer is ephemeral) but in-container persistence and self-modification are possible for the container's lifetime.
attack_scenario: An attacker achieves arbitrary write through some other defect.
Because /app is writable by uid node, they overwrite a required module and wait for the next in-container reload, or tamper with logs in /app/logs which is a host bind mount in compose.
findings.attacker_role: Attacker with a code-execution or arbitrary-write foothold
findings.preconditions: A separate primary vulnerability; none was identified in this audit.

impact.confidentiality: Log tampering could destroy forensic evidence.
impact.business_impact: Reduced containment and auditability after a breach.

steps: Read Dockerfile:28-39 and docker-compose.yml.
reproduction.expected_result: Application code owned by root and read-only to the runtime user; only /app/logs writable.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Image build was not performed in the sandbox.

findings.existing_controls: Non-root USER node, production-only dependencies, multi-stage build, .dockerignore excludes .env and logs, compose sets init: true.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Restrict chown to /app/logs only; add HEALTHCHECK; in compose add read_only: true with a tmpfs for /tmp, cap_drop: [ALL], and security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true].
alternatives: Distroless base image
Run under a read-only rootfs with an explicit writable log volume
regression_tests: Container smoke test asserting the app starts with a read-only rootfs.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: The runtime user can write only to the log volume.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Read-only rootfs and narrowed ownership can break runtime paths (e.g. npm cache, Vite artifacts) and must be validated by building and running the image.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Defence-in-depth only; no primary exploit path was found, so severity is Low and reachable=false.

findings.title: Compose publishes the dashboard port on all host interfaces by default
findings.root_cause: A bare host:container mapping binds 0.0.0.0 and, on Linux, Docker's iptables rules commonly bypass host firewall policy, publishing a plaintext-HTTP origin directly to the Internet.
findings.violated_invariant: The Node origin should be reachable only from the reverse proxy when a proxy is the intended entry point — as docs/security-deployment.md itself instructs.
findings.data_flow: Internet -> host:WEB_PORT -> container:WEB_PORT -> Express (HTTP, cookie sessions without Secure when WEB_HTTPS=false).
attack_scenario: Operator deploys with the shipped compose file behind Cloudflare.
The origin port remains directly reachable, so an attacker bypasses the edge entirely — skipping any WAF/rate limiting there — and, with WEB_HTTPS=false, session cookies traverse plaintext HTTP.
findings.preconditions: Public host with the default compose file.

impact.confidentiality: Session cookie interception on plaintext HTTP paths.
impact.business_impact: Loss of the intended edge security boundary.

steps: Read docker-compose.yml:11-12 and compare with docs/security-deployment.md's instruction to keep the origin private.

findings.existing_controls: Documentation advises keeping the origin private, but the shipped default contradicts it.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Bind to loopback by default: "127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT:-8080}:${WEB_PORT:-8080}", and document how to widen it deliberately.
alternatives: Put the app on an internal compose network with the proxy as the only publisher.
regression_tests: docker compose config assertion on the published address.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Default deployment is not Internet-reachable without an explicit operator choice.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Loopback binding breaks setups where the proxy runs on a different host; the operator must confirm topology.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Some operators intentionally expose the port directly (documented as acceptable for private networks), so this is a default-hardening issue rather than a vulnerability per se.
findings.limitations: Depends on host firewall configuration not visible here.

findings.title: run.js writes an unignored log.txt and spawns npm through a shell
findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.root_cause: The helper captures the full stdout/stderr of npm install/build/start into repo-root log.txt. .gitignore covers *.log but not log.txt, so build output — which includes application startup logging — can be committed. shell: true is used with a fixed argv, so there is no injection today, but it is an unnecessary shell hop.
findings.violated_invariant: Runtime output must not land in version-controlled paths, and child processes should not invoke a shell without need.
findings.data_flow: npm run start stdout (which includes pino stdout stream output from src/services/logger.js) -> log.txt in the repository working tree -> potentially git add.
attack_scenario: An operator runs node run.js on the server, then later commits the tree.
log.txt containing startup diagnostics is pushed to the repository.
Although logger.js redacts and sanitises its own output, any third-party dependency writing directly to stdout is not covered by that redaction.
findings.attacker_role: Anyone with repository read access after an accidental commit
findings.preconditions: run.js used and the tree committed.
findings.affected_deployment: Deployments using run.js rather than npm start / Docker.

impact.confidentiality: Possible disclosure of operational diagnostics in a shared repository.

steps: Read run.js:5-7 and .gitignore; confirm 'log.txt' does not match any ignore pattern (git check-ignore log.txt returns non-zero).
reproduction.expected_result: Runtime logs written under LOG_DIR and ignored.
reproduction.poc_constraints: run.js was not executed (it would trigger npm install and start the app).

findings.existing_controls: logger.js redacts and sanitises its own records; .dockerignore excludes *.log (but likewise not log.txt).

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Write to logs/run.log (already ignored) and add log.txt to .gitignore/.dockerignore; drop shell: true since argv is fixed.
alternatives: Remove run.js in favour of documented npm scripts.
regression_tests: Assert git check-ignore succeeds for the chosen log path.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: No runtime output can be committed.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Path change plus ignore entries; no behavioural risk.
findings.false_positive_analysis: No command injection is possible here — the command and arguments are hardcoded literals — so this is not reported as an injection finding.

findings.title: Encrypted payloads embed an 8-hex-character fingerprint derived from the encryption key
findings.root_cause: Every ciphertext row stores SHA256(key)[0:8], an unsalted 32-bit commitment to the key, needed to select the right key during rotation.
findings.violated_invariant: Ciphertext metadata should not commit to the key material.
findings.data_flow: encrypt() -> bots.encrypted_password column -> anyone with DB read access.
attack_scenario: An attacker with read access to the bots table obtains the fingerprint.

Because the key is 32 bytes of entropy, brute-forcing preimages is infeasible; the practical value is limited to confirming whether two databases or two rows use the same key, and to verifying a guessed key offline without touching the service.
The offline-verification property matters only if key candidates come from elsewhere (e.g. a partially leaked .env).
findings.preconditions: DB compromise, which already implies access to the ciphertexts.

impact.confidentiality: Marginal — enables key-candidate confirmation and cross-deployment key correlation.

steps: Read src/services/encryption.js:19-57.
reproduction.expected_result: A random key identifier (key id) stored alongside the key, not derived from it.
reproduction.observed_result: Fingerprint derived directly from the key.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No key recovery is feasible; reporting anything stronger would be inaccurate.

findings.existing_controls: GCM authentication and 256-bit key entropy make the fingerprint useless for direct recovery.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Optional: replace the derived fingerprint with an opaque random key-id configured alongside the key (e.g. ENCRYPTION_KEY_ID), keeping the same versioned payload layout.
alternatives: Keep as-is and accept the residual risk; document the rationale.
regression_tests: Round-trip and rotation tests already exist in tests/encryption.test.js and must keep passing.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Rotation still works without committing to key material.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Changing the payload format would require migrating every stored ciphertext; the security gain does not justify automated change.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Deliberately rated Informational — this is a recognised, common design for key rotation and does not weaken AES-256-GCM.

findings.title: Database schema and documentation provide no least-privilege role guidance for the application user
findings.root_cause: The schema is applied with `psql "$DATABASE_URL"`, implying the application's own connection role is also the DDL owner. No GRANT statements, no separate migration role, and no revocation of unneeded privileges are provided.
findings.violated_invariant: The runtime database role should hold only the DML privileges it needs.
findings.data_flow: DATABASE_URL role -> CREATE EXTENSION/CREATE TABLE at install time and SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE at runtime.
attack_scenario: If a SQL injection or credential leak ever occurs, the compromised role can also DROP tables, create functions, or use pgcrypto — turning a data-read incident into destruction of the bot fleet and audit trail.
No injection path was found in this audit, so this is preventative.
findings.attacker_role: Attacker who obtains DB credentials or an injection primitive

impact.integrity: Would allow schema destruction and audit-log tampering (bot_activity_log is the only audit trail).

steps: Read db/schema.sql and package.json's db:schema script; grep for GRANT/REVOKE — none present.
reproduction.expected_result: A documented owner/migration role distinct from the runtime role, with explicit grants.

findings.existing_controls: Transport is protected by enforced verified TLS (src/config/database.js); all queries are parameterised; statement_timeout is set.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Document and optionally script a two-role setup: an owner role for migrations, and an app role granted only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the specific tables plus USAGE on sequences.
alternatives: Row-level security keyed on created_by for defence in depth.
regression_tests: Integration test asserting the app role cannot execute DDL.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Runtime role cannot alter the schema.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Requires coordinated database administration outside the repository.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Purely preventative hardening; no exploit path was demonstrated, hence Informational.
findings.limitations: The operator may already run a least-privilege role; the repository simply does not say.

findings.title: Unused WebNotifier module publishes owner-less SSE events (dead code with a latent access-control hazard)
findings.excerpt:
publishCreated(instance) { publish('bot:created', { snapshot: snapshot(instance) }); },
publishUpdated(instance) { publish('bot:updated', { snapshot: snapshot(instance) }); },
publishDeleted(botId) { publish('bot:deleted', { botId }); },
findings.root_cause: The module duplicates instanceEvents.js but omits ownerId. grep across src, index.js, and tests shows no importer other than the module's own export line, so it never executes.
findings.violated_invariant: N/A at this commit — the code is unreachable.
attack_scenario: No attack is possible at this commit because the module is never instantiated. It is recorded because wiring it would immediately realise EG-002.

steps: grep -rn "createWebNotifier\|attachWebNotifier" src index.js tests -> only definitions and the export inside WebNotifier.js itself.
reproduction.expected_result: Either the module is used with correct scoping, or it is removed.

findings.existing_controls: The live path (instanceEvents.js) always includes ownerId.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Delete the module, or add ownerId to its payloads before any future use.
alternatives: Merge it into instanceEvents.js so there is a single publisher.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: Only one SSE publisher exists and it always attaches ownerId.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Deleting a module may break an intended but unfinished feature; a maintainer should decide.
findings.false_positive_analysis: Classified false_positive as a *current* vulnerability precisely because reachability analysis disproves exploitability at this commit. It is retained as a hardening note and cross-referenced from EG-002 rather than dropped.
findings.limitations: Reachability was established by grep over the repository; dynamic require of this path does not occur (the only dynamic requires are the Discord command/event loaders, which read different directories).

findings.title: Transitive dependency qs 6.15.3 carries two moderate advisories reachable through Express query parsing
findings.root_cause: The pinned qs version is within the vulnerable range of GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx (array-limit bypass via bracket-key comma parsing) and GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g (DoS via attacker-controlled isBuffer).
findings.violated_invariant: Dependencies with known advisories should be patched or demonstrably unreachable.
findings.data_flow: Any HTTP request -> Express default query parser (qs) -> req.query. No application route reads req.query (verified by grep), but parsing happens before the handler regardless.
attack_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker sends requests with crafted query strings to any route, including /healthz and the SPA fallback.
The parsing work occurs even though the result is discarded, so the DoS advisory's CPU/memory cost is incurred by the process.
The array-limit bypass has no application impact here because no route consumes req.query.
findings.preconditions: Network reachability to the web port.

impact.availability: Parsing-cost amplification against a process that also supervises all Minecraft bots.
impact.business_impact: Potential bot fleet downtime under a targeted flood.

steps: npm audit --audit-level=moderate.
grep -rn 'req.query' src -> no matches, establishing partial non-reachability.
reproduction.observed_result: qs 6.15.3 flagged with two moderate advisories.
reproduction.poc_constraints: No malicious payload was sent to any service, per the safety rules; exploitability was reasoned about, not demonstrated.

findings.existing_controls: No route reads req.query; body size capped at 32kb. There is no cap on URL/query length at the application layer.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Run npm audit fix (non-force) to move qs to a patched patch-level release within the existing semver range, and re-run the full test suite.
alternatives: app.set('query parser', 'simple') to use Node's built-in querystring and bypass qs entirely for parsing
Add a lockfile override pinning a patched qs
regression_tests: Existing suite; add a test asserting the app responds normally to a long/complex query string.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: npm audit reports no moderate-or-higher advisories and all tests pass.

findings.auto_fix_reason: npm audit fix (never --force) is low risk here since the fix is within the existing range, but the lockfile change must be verified by a full test run before release. Major-version upgrades must not be applied.
findings.false_positive_analysis: The array-limit advisory is effectively a non-issue for this application because req.query is never consumed; only the parsing-cost advisory is meaningfully reachable. Severity is therefore held at Medium rather than raised.
findings.limitations: Advisory severity was taken from npm audit output; no independent exploit validation was attempted.

findings.title: Config module calls process.exit(1) at require time, making the test suite silently env-dependent
findings.category: Fail-safe design / testability of security controls
findings.root_cause: Configuration validation failure terminates the process during module evaluation. Any test that transitively requires src/config without the full env set exits the worker rather than failing an assertion.
findings.violated_invariant: Security-relevant test suites must fail loudly and for the right reason.
findings.data_flow: require('src/config') -> validation -> process.exit(1) -> node:test worker exits with code 1.
attack_scenario: Not attacker-driven. The operational risk is that `npm test` in CI without the dummy env reports 10 failing suites — including securityAuthorization, securityEgress, securityLimits, and securityPersistence — with an exit-code failure that masks whether the security invariants themselves passed.
A maintainer could mistake an env problem for a real regression, or worse, mark those suites as flaky and stop trusting them.

impact.integrity: Security regressions could go unnoticed if these suites are habitually red.
impact.availability: None in production (fail-closed at startup is otherwise correct behaviour).
impact.business_impact: Erosion of the security regression safety net.

steps: npm test with no env -> exit 1, 10/28 suites fail with '[CONFIG] Fatal: Missing required env var: ENCRYPTION_KEY'.
Re-run with dummy ENCRYPTION_KEY/ADMIN_USER_IDS/DISCORD_TOKEN/DISCORD_CLIENT_ID -> 173/173 pass, exit 0.
reproduction.expected_result: Tests pass or fail on their own assertions.
reproduction.poc_constraints: Only dummy values were used; no real secrets.

findings.existing_controls: Fail-closed startup validation is the correct production behaviour; only the exit-during-require coupling is problematic.

fix_strategy.minimal_patch: Export a loadConfig() that throws, and call process.exit(1) only from index.js's startup path; alternatively ship a tests/.env fixture or a node:test setup file that supplies dummy values.
alternatives: Document the required test env in README and CI.
regression_tests: Assert that requiring the config module with a missing var throws rather than exiting.
fix_strategy.acceptance_criteria: npm test passes from a clean checkout with no manual env setup.

findings.auto_fix_reason: Moving the exit out of module scope changes startup semantics for every consumer of the config module and must be reviewed against the fail-closed requirement.
findings.false_positive_analysis: This is not a production vulnerability — fail-closed startup is desirable. It is reported because it directly degrades the verifiability of the repository's own security tests.
evidence_refs: npm test output (10 suites failing without env; 173/173 passing with env)

fix_order.rationale: Confirmed live cross-user data leak on an authenticated stream; smallest, safest patch with the highest immediate value. No dependencies.
Same file and function as EG-001; making the SSE filter fail-closed should be done in the same change so the publisher contract is fixed once.
Resolve the unused owner-less publisher immediately after the filter is hardened, so the two cannot drift apart again.
Restore a trustworthy `npm test` before landing further security changes, so every subsequent fix has a working regression gate.
Dependency patch is independent of application logic; do it early with the now-reliable test suite. Use npm audit fix without --force.
Trust-proxy configuration must precede any global rate limiting, otherwise the new limiter inherits the same wrong key.
Add global and per-route limits once req.ip is correct.
Origin/CSRF enforcement touches the same middleware stack as the limiter; land it together with the web-layer changes.
One-line algorithm pin in the token service; independent.
Key separation is a breaking env change; sequence it after the algorithm pin so token-service changes ship together, and coordinate with an operator.
Token TTL/distribution policy change follows the key-management work.
Independent additive pruning in the limiter module; do after EG-008 so limiter behaviour is settled.
Deployment default hardening; requires operator topology confirmation.
Container hardening should follow the compose binding change so both are validated in one image build/run cycle.
Documentation/administration change with no code coupling.
Accept or defer; would require ciphertext migration and yields minimal benefit.

limitations: No provided security-audit-result.schema.json exists in the repository or workspace, so formal schema validation could not be executed; only JSON well-formedness was verified with a parser.
Node 22 was used because Node 24 was unavailable, while package.json requires >=24.
No PostgreSQL, Discord, or Minecraft endpoint was contacted; findings depending on those runtimes are rated likely/potential.
The frontend was not installed or built; frontend conclusions rest on static source review plus a lockfile audit that reported zero vulnerabilities.
Lockfiles were inspected selectively for security-relevant packages rather than entry by entry; integrity hashes were not independently verified against the registry.
No load, fuzz, brute-force, or destructive testing was performed, in accordance with the safety rules; availability findings are reasoned rather than measured.
Source code was not modified during the audit, so findings requiring code changes to demonstrate (notably EG-002) are supported by static proof only.
Findings describe commit 66cf76b0d9517238e6ee4a23a2686bf652516d44 only and make no claim about any later state.
audit_status_reason: All in-scope files were enumerated and either audited or explicitly recorded as partially audited or skipped, and every limitation is documented. Status is 'partial' rather than 'completed' because the frontend install/build commands and Node 24 verification could not be executed, and the requested output schema was unavailable for validation.
